title: Liquid IV vs Propel: Which Is Better for Hydration and Hangovers?
excerpt: Liquid IV and Propel compared: sodium, potassium, sugar, price, and taste. Which one actually rehydrates you after drinking, and when Propel is all you need.
metaDescription: Liquid IV vs Propel compared: sodium, potassium, sugar, and price. Which one rehydrates you better after drinking, and when Propel is all you need.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Liquid I.V. and Propel are not really the same kind of drink. Liquid I.V. is a rehydration mix built on the same idea as the oral rehydration solutions doctors use for dehydration: a fair amount of sodium, a good dose of potassium, and a small amount of sugar that helps your gut pull water in. Propel is a zero-calorie, lightly salted vitamin water from the Gatorade family. If you're properly dried out, whether from a long night of drinking, a hot day, heavy sweating, or a stomach bug, Liquid I.V. is the better tool. If you just want something tastier than water that you'll actually drink all day, with no sugar and no calories, Propel is the better fit. Neither one cures a hangover.

**The quick picks:**

- **Morning after a big night, mild vomiting, hot weather, or a long sweaty workout:** Liquid I.V. (original), one stick in 16 ounces of water, sipped over half an hour or so.
- **Everyday hydration, light exercise, or replacing soda:** Propel.
- **Watching sugar but still want a real electrolyte dose:** Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free, which sits between the two.
- **Mild hangover and Propel is what's in the fridge:** drink it, plus some water and a salty snack. That covers most of what a mild hangover needs from a drink.
- **High blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or a low-salt diet:** ask your doctor before using Liquid I.V. regularly. Propel's sodium is modest, but it still counts toward your daily total.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article compares consumer drinks and explains general research in plain words. It is not medical advice. **Get medical help instead of reaching for an electrolyte drink if** you can't keep fluids down for most of a day, you've vomited repeatedly or see blood in vomit or stool, you've barely urinated in 8 hours or more, or you feel faint, confused, or dizzy when you stand. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room** if someone who has been drinking is very hard to wake, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and no drink mix helps with that. **Talk to your doctor before using electrolyte mixes regularly** if you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or diabetes, or you take medicines that change your sodium or potassium levels, such as some blood pressure pills and water pills.

## Liquid I.V. vs Propel: The Numbers Side by Side

Most of the difference comes down to three things: how much sodium is in a serving, how much potassium, and whether there's any sugar. Here are approximate label figures for the common versions. Both brands adjust formulas, flavors, and serving sizes from time to time, so check the package you're actually holding.

| Per serving (approx.) | Serving | Sodium | Potassium | Sugar | Calories |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Liquid I.V. Hydration Multiplier (original) | 1 stick in 16 fl oz water | ~500 mg | ~370 mg | ~11 g | ~45 |
| Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free | 1 stick in 16 fl oz water | ~500 mg | ~370 mg | 0 g | ~15 or less |
| Propel Fitness Water (bottle) | 16.9 fl oz bottle | Roughly 200 to 300 mg | Small, well under 100 mg | 0 g | 0 |
| Propel powder packet | 1 packet in 16.9 fl oz water | Similar to the bottle | Small | 0 g | 0 |

A few other differences that don't fit neatly in the table:

| | Liquid I.V. | Propel |
|---|---|---|
| Owner | Unilever | PepsiCo (part of the Gatorade family) |
| Sweetener | Cane sugar and dextrose (original); allulose and other non-sugar sweeteners in Sugar-Free | Sucralose and acesulfame potassium |
| Added vitamins | Vitamin C and several B vitamins | Vitamins C and E plus some B vitamins (varies by product) |
| Format | Powder sticks only | Ready-to-drink bottles and powder packets |
| Taste | Sweet, a bit salty, fairly strong flavor | Light, mildly sweet, closer to flavored water |
| Typical price per serving | Roughly $1 to $1.50 | Often well under $1 |
| Where to buy | Grocery, big-box, pharmacies, warehouse clubs | Grocery, gas stations, big-box, pharmacies |

The headline: **per serving, Liquid I.V. has roughly twice the sodium of Propel and several times the potassium, plus a small amount of sugar.** Propel has no sugar and no calories. Everything else in this comparison follows from that.

## Why the Sugar Actually Matters (and Why It Isn't a Flaw)

It's tempting to look at that table and decide Propel wins because it has zero sugar. For everyday sipping, that's a fair way to see it. For rehydration, though, the small amount of sugar in Liquid I.V. is doing a job.

Your small intestine has a transporter that moves sodium and glucose into your body together, as a pair. Water follows them. This is the basic principle behind oral rehydration solution (ORS), the simple salt-and-sugar drink the World Health Organization has promoted for decades to treat dehydration from diarrhea. It's one of the better-established ideas in rehydration medicine.

What this means in practice:

- **A drink with both sodium and a modest amount of glucose** helps your gut absorb water faster than plain water would. That's the idea behind Liquid I.V.'s original formula, which the brand markets as "Cellular Transport Technology."
- **A drink with sodium but no glucose**, like Propel or Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free, still gives you some sodium and fluid, but you lose that pairing effect.
- **A drink with lots of sugar**, like regular soda or juice, can actually work against you. Too much sugar pulls water into the gut rather than out of it, which is why very sugary drinks can make loose stools worse.

Liquid I.V.'s roughly 11 grams of sugar per stick is about a third of what's in a 20-ounce regular sports drink. It's a moderate dose, enough to help absorption without being a sugar bomb. For a deeper look at how the original formula holds up, see our [Liquid I.V. for hangovers review](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-for-hangover).

One honest caveat: medical ORS (the WHO formula) has more sodium relative to its volume than Liquid I.V. does, so Liquid I.V. is "ORS-inspired" rather than a true medical rehydration solution. For a healthy adult with a hangover, that difference is minor.

## Liquid I.V. vs Propel for a Hangover

### What a drink can and can't do for a hangover

Alcohol makes you pee more by suppressing a hormone called vasopressin, which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. Add in sweating in a warm bar, maybe some vomiting, and not drinking much water all night, and you can wake up genuinely short on fluid and salt. That part of a hangover (thirst, dry mouth, a dull headache, feeling lightheaded when you stand) is what an electrolyte drink can help with. Our guide on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) goes through the details.

But dehydration is only one piece. Hangovers also come from alcohol's by-products, especially acetaldehyde, from disrupted sleep, from inflammation, and from irritation of your stomach lining. Research on hangovers has found that how dehydrated people are doesn't line up closely with how bad their hangover feels. So the honest expectation is this: **the right drink can take the edge off the thirsty, headachy, wiped-out part of a hangover. It won't fix nausea, fatigue, or brain fog on its own.**

### When Liquid I.V. is the better choice

Pick Liquid I.V. when you have real fluid losses to make up:

- You drank heavily, or for many hours.
- You vomited, or you've had loose stools.
- It was a hot night, you danced a lot, or you were outdoors in the sun.
- You feel dizzy when you stand up, your urine is dark, or you've barely peed since waking.

In those situations, the higher sodium and potassium plus the glucose pairing make a noticeable difference compared with lightly salted water. Mix one stick in the full 16 ounces of water (don't make it stronger), and sip it over 20 to 30 minutes rather than chugging it, especially if your stomach is unsettled.

### When Propel is fine

Propel is a reasonable choice when:

- It was a moderate night and you mostly feel tired and thirsty.
- You want to keep sipping something through the day without adding sugar or calories.
- You don't like the stronger, saltier taste of rehydration mixes and you'll drink more of something lighter.

That last point matters more than people think. The best hangover drink is often the one you'll actually finish. If two bottles of Propel go down easily and a Liquid I.V. sits half-full on the counter, Propel wins that morning. Pair it with a salty snack (crackers, toast, a bowl of soup) and you'll close much of the sodium gap.

### Using both

There's no reason you can't combine them. A common, sensible approach after a big night: one Liquid I.V. in the morning to cover the electrolyte deficit, then Propel or plain water for the rest of the day. That gives you a solid dose of sodium and potassium up front without stacking two or three high-sodium sticks. For the full picture of morning-after fluids, see [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking).

## Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free vs Propel

This is the comparison many people actually mean when they search "Liquid IV vs Propel," because both are marketed to people avoiding sugar.

Both drop the glucose, so neither gets the full sodium-glucose absorption boost. The difference that remains is the dose:

- **Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free** keeps roughly the same sodium and potassium as the original, about 500 mg and 370 mg. It's a meaningfully stronger electrolyte drink.
- **Propel** has well under that on both counts. It's flavored water with some electrolytes, not a rehydration mix.

So if you're on a low-carb or keto diet, you're diabetic and watching blood sugar (and your doctor is fine with the sodium), or you just don't want sugar, but you still want a real electrolyte dose after a big night or a long workout, Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free is the stronger of the two. If you only want a pleasant zero-calorie drink to sip at your desk, Propel is cheaper and lighter.

Some people find the sweeteners in either product don't sit well with them, especially on an already upset stomach. Sugar alcohols and some non-sugar sweeteners can cause bloating or loose stools in large amounts. If that's you, the original Liquid I.V. or a [homemade electrolyte drink](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) may be gentler.

## Propel vs Liquid I.V. for Workouts and Everyday Hydration

Outside of hangovers, the choice depends on how much you sweat.

**For light to moderate exercise** (a 30 to 60 minute gym session, a jog, a yoga class), most healthy people don't need special electrolyte drinks at all. Water and your next meal cover it. If flavored water helps you drink more, Propel is a good fit. It was originally marketed as "fitness water" for exactly this use.

**For long or very sweaty sessions** (over an hour, hot conditions, endurance events, or if you're a "salty sweater" who finds white streaks on your clothes), you lose more sodium than Propel replaces. Liquid I.V. covers more of that. People doing very long or very hot sessions often go even higher on sodium, which is where products like LMNT come in. Our [LMNT vs Liquid I.V. comparison](/never-hungover/lmnt-vs-liquid-iv) covers that end of the range.

**For all-day sipping**, Propel makes more sense. Drinking three or four Liquid I.V. sticks a day would add something like 1,500 to 2,000 mg of sodium on top of your normal diet. The US Dietary Guidelines suggest keeping total sodium under 2,300 mg a day for most adults, and most Americans already eat more than that. Propel's lower sodium is easier to fit into a daily routine.

## Taste, Convenience, and Cost

These aren't the most important factors, but they're why people stick with one or the other.

**Taste.** Propel tastes like lightly sweetened flavored water. It's easy to drink in large amounts. Liquid I.V. is sweeter and noticeably saltier, closer to a sports drink. Some people love it, and some find it too strong, especially when their stomach is off. If you find Liquid I.V. too intense, try it with slightly more water or over ice. That dilutes it a little, but you still get the full dose of electrolytes if you finish the glass.

**Convenience.** Propel comes ready to drink in bottles, which you can grab at almost any gas station or grocery store at 1 a.m. on the way home. It also comes in powder packets sized for a 16.9-ounce water bottle. Liquid I.V. only comes as powder sticks, so you need water and a container, but the sticks are small and easy to keep in a bag, a desk drawer, or a travel kit.

**Cost.** Propel is usually the cheaper option per serving, especially in powder form or in big multipacks. Liquid I.V. typically runs about a dollar to a dollar and a half per stick, depending on pack size and where you buy it. Warehouse clubs and big online packs bring both down. Prices change often, so compare per-serving costs where you shop.

## Honest Pros and Cons

### Liquid I.V.

**Pros**

- Real rehydration dose: about 500 mg sodium and 370 mg potassium per stick.
- Small amount of sugar that helps absorption, based on the oral rehydration principle.
- Compact sticks that travel well.
- Sugar-Free version available for people avoiding sugar.

**Cons**

- More expensive per serving than Propel.
- The sodium adds up quickly if you have more than one a day.
- Stronger, saltier taste that some people find hard to drink when nauseous.
- Powder only, so you need water and a container.
- Contains sugar in the original version (about 11 grams per stick), which some people want to avoid.

### Propel

**Pros**

- Zero sugar and zero calories.
- Light, easy-to-drink taste.
- Cheap, especially in powder packets.
- Available almost everywhere, ready to drink.
- Easy to fit into everyday hydration without adding much sodium.

**Cons**

- Much lower sodium and potassium than a rehydration mix.
- No glucose, so it misses the sodium-glucose absorption boost.
- Not well suited to real dehydration from vomiting, diarrhea, or long sweaty sessions.
- Uses artificial sweeteners (sucralose and acesulfame potassium), which some people prefer to avoid.

## How These Two Compare With Other Options

Liquid I.V. and Propel sit at different ends of the electrolyte-drink range. Roughly, from lightest to strongest:

1. **Plain water.** Fine for mild thirst, especially with food.
2. **Propel and similar zero-calorie electrolyte waters.** A step up from water, mainly helpful because they're easy to drink more of.
3. **Regular sports drinks** like Gatorade. Moderate sodium, lots of sugar. Our [Liquid I.V. vs Gatorade comparison](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-vs-gatorade) covers that matchup.
4. **ORS-style mixes** like Liquid I.V. and similar products. Meaningful sodium and potassium with a moderate amount of glucose.
5. **Medical oral rehydration solutions** like Pedialyte and DripDrop. Designed for real dehydration from illness.

If you want a broader ranking, our [electrolyte drinks for hangovers comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) puts the main options side by side.

## Who Should Be Careful With Electrolyte Drinks

For most healthy adults, an occasional Liquid I.V. or a few bottles of Propel are not a concern. A few groups should check with a doctor first, mainly because of the sodium and potassium:

- **High blood pressure.** Extra sodium can raise blood pressure in some people.
- **Kidney disease.** Damaged kidneys can struggle to clear extra potassium and sodium.
- **Heart failure.** People with heart failure are often told to limit both salt and fluids.
- **Medicines that affect sodium or potassium.** Examples include some blood pressure medicines (such as ACE inhibitors and ARBs), potassium-sparing water pills, and some others. Too much potassium can be dangerous for people on these drugs.
- **Diabetes.** The original Liquid I.V. contains sugar. The sugar-free version or Propel avoids that, but it's still worth checking with your care team.

If any of these apply to you, ask your doctor or pharmacist which drink, if any, is right for you and how often.

## A Smarter Hangover Plan Than Any Single Drink

If you find yourself comparing hydration drinks because you regularly wake up feeling rough, it's worth stepping back. The habits with the best evidence for a better morning aren't about what you drink the next day. They're about the night before:

- **Eat a real meal before and while you drink.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream.
- **Pace yourself.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour. Drinking faster than that lets alcohol build up.
- **Alternate alcohol with water.** A glass of water between drinks reduces how much you drink overall and keeps you a bit more hydrated.
- **Pick lighter drinks.** Darker spirits like bourbon and red wine tend to have more congeners, by-products linked to worse hangovers in some studies.
- **Sleep.** Alcohol disrupts sleep, and poor sleep makes everything feel worse.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through each of these in more detail.

Some people also add a supplement to their routine. The one we cover most here is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers on its own, and it doesn't replace water, food, or drinking less. It also does nothing for dehydration, so it's a different tool from Liquid I.V. or Propel, not a replacement. If you want to try it, the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a simple single-ingredient option, and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) adds electrolytes and other ingredients to the mix. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- **Liquid I.V. is a rehydration mix. Propel is flavored water with some electrolytes.** They do different jobs.
- For real dehydration after a big night, heavy sweating, or a stomach bug, **Liquid I.V. is the better choice**, thanks to its higher sodium and potassium and its small, useful dose of sugar.
- For everyday sipping, light exercise, or replacing soda, **Propel is cheaper, lighter, and has no sugar or calories**.
- **Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free** is the middle ground: no sugar, but a much bigger electrolyte dose than Propel.
- Neither one cures a hangover. They help with the dehydration part only.
- If you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or take medicines that affect sodium or potassium, ask your doctor before making either one a regular habit.
- If someone can't keep fluids down, is confused, or is hard to wake after drinking, skip the drink mix and get medical help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Propel as good as Liquid IV?**

Not for rehydration. Liquid I.V. carries roughly twice the sodium and several times the potassium per serving, plus a small amount of sugar that helps your gut absorb sodium and water. Propel is a lightly salted, zero-calorie vitamin water. It's a good everyday drink and a fine swap for soda, but if you're properly dried out after a night of drinking, a hot day, or a stomach bug, Liquid I.V. (or another oral-rehydration-style mix) does the job better.

**Which is better for a hangover, Propel or Liquid IV?**

Liquid I.V. is the better pick if you're genuinely dehydrated, because its sodium, potassium, and glucose recipe is closer to the medical oral rehydration solutions used for dehydration. Propel works fine for a mild hangover where you mainly need to drink more fluid and it's what you have on hand. Neither one fixes the nausea, fatigue, or brain fog that come from alcohol itself, so food, sleep, and time still matter.

**Does Propel have enough electrolytes?**

For everyday drinking and light exercise, yes. A bottle or packet has a modest amount of sodium, roughly in the low hundreds of milligrams, and a small amount of potassium. That's enough to make it more useful than plain water for some people, but it's well below what a rehydration mix like Liquid I.V. provides. If you're sweating heavily for hours or have lost fluid through vomiting or diarrhea, Propel alone is on the light side.

**Is Liquid IV Sugar-Free the same as Propel?**

They're closer, but not the same. Both have no sugar, so both give up the glucose-sodium absorption boost that makes the original Liquid I.V. work like an oral rehydration solution. The sugar-free Liquid I.V. still carries much more sodium and potassium than Propel per serving. Propel is cheaper and lighter. Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free is the stronger electrolyte drink without the sugar.

**Can I drink Propel or Liquid IV every day?**

Most healthy adults can drink Propel daily without trouble, since its sodium is modest. Liquid I.V. adds around 500 mg of sodium per stick, which adds up quickly alongside a normal diet, so one a day is plenty for most people and many don't need it at all on days they aren't sweating or ill. If you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or are on a low-salt diet, ask your doctor before making either a daily habit.

**Should I drink Propel or Liquid IV before drinking alcohol?**

Being well hydrated before you drink is sensible, and a glass of either is fine. But there's no good evidence that pre-loading electrolytes prevents a hangover. The habits that matter more are eating a real meal, pacing your drinks, and alternating alcohol with water. Save the stronger mix, Liquid I.V., for the morning after if you actually feel dried out.

**Which is cheaper, Propel or Liquid IV?**

Propel is usually cheaper per serving, often well under a dollar for a powder packet and around a dollar or less per bottle in multipacks. Liquid I.V. typically costs about a dollar to a dollar and a half per stick depending on pack size and store. Prices change a lot with sales and warehouse-club packs, so compare the per-serving price where you shop.
